title: PersistentVolumes & Claims
summary: PVs are cluster storage, PVCs are requests for it: provisioning, binding, access modes, reclaim policies and phases.

sections.heading: PV and PVC: the two objects

blocks.text: Lockers vanish with a bay, so for lasting cargo the port rents **warehouse units** (PersistentVolumes). A unit belongs to the whole port, like a ship, while a **rental request** (PersistentVolumeClaim) is filed inside one company yard and consumes a unit, like a bay. The unit records how it is built (NFS, cloud disk); tenants only see their request. Bays can only use requests from their own yard.
The PersistentVolume subsystem separates **how storage is provided** from **how it is consumed**.

steps.text: A **PersistentVolume** is a piece of storage in the cluster, provisioned by an administrator or dynamically.
A **PersistentVolumeClaim** is a user's request for storage. The control plane binds it to a matching PV, one to one.
With dynamic provisioning, the claim's **StorageClass** creates a PV for it.
A Pod mounts the claim as a volume, and the data outlives the Pod.

rows: A piece of storage, created by an admin or dynamically via a StorageClass. Its lifecycle is independent of any Pod.
Like a node: a cluster resource
A user's request for storage: a size and access modes.
Like a Pod: it consumes PV resources

items: A PV is a **cluster** resource; PVCs are **namespaced** objects, and a Pod can only use claims from its **own namespace**.
A PV records the storage implementation details (NFS, iSCSI, a cloud provider's disk...). Users only deal with the claim.
StorageClasses let admins offer storage that differs in more than size and access mode (performance, for example).

blocks.text: Units appear two ways: the admin builds them in advance (static), or the warehouse rental catalog builds one when no unit fits (dynamic). A clerk then pairs each request with one unit, exclusively, and you get at least the size you asked for. If nothing fits, the request waits. When a request is torn up, the unit's reclaim policy decides its fate. Units or requests still in use can't be removed early; they sit `Terminating`.

items: **Static provisioning**: an admin pre-creates PVs that describe real storage.
**Dynamic provisioning**: if no static PV matches, the cluster may provision one based on the PVC's StorageClass. A claim requesting class `""` opts out of dynamic provisioning.
**Binding**: a control-plane loop matches a new PVC to a PV. Binding is **one-to-one** and exclusive, recorded with a `claimRef`. You always get at least what you asked for, possibly more.
A claim with no matching PV stays **unbound indefinitely**, and binds when a suitable PV appears (100Gi requested, only 50Gi PVs: it waits).
**Using**: a Pod lists the claim under `volumes`; the bound PV is the user's for as long as they need it.
**Reclaiming**: when the PVC is deleted, the PV's reclaim policy decides what happens next.

blocks.text: **Storage Object in Use Protection**: deleting a PVC that a Pod uses, or a PV bound to a PVC, is postponed. The object shows `Terminating` with the `kubernetes.io/pvc-protection` or `kubernetes.io/pv-protection` finalizer.

Each unit lists the ways it can be opened. **RWO**: read-write from one ship, though several bays on that ship can share it. **ROX**: read-only from many ships. **RWX**: read-write from many ships. **RWOP**: read-write by a single bay in the whole port. A unit is opened one way at a time. These modes mostly help match requests to units; only RWOP truly guards writes.

rows: Read-write by a **single node**. Several Pods on that node can still use it.
Read-write by a **single Pod** in the whole cluster. CSI volumes only.

items: Each PV lists the modes its backend supports. For example, `HostPath` supports RWO only, while `NFS` supports RWO, ROX and RWX.
A volume is mounted with **one access mode at a time**, even if it supports several.
Access modes are used to **match** PVCs to PVs. Apart from RWOP, they don't enforce write protection once mounted.
Because PVCs are namespaced, sharing a claim with ROX/RWX only works **within one namespace**.

blocks.text: When a tenant ends a rental, the unit's reclaim policy kicks in. **Retain**: the unit stays, marked Released, until an admin clears it out. **Delete**: the unit and the storage behind it are demolished. **Recycle** (deprecated): a quick sweep, then it's rentable again. Units built on demand by the rental catalog copy its policy, which defaults to Delete.

rows: PV stays and becomes **Released**. Not reusable until an admin cleans it up.
PV object **and** the backing storage asset are removed
Basic scrub (`rm -rf /thevolume/*`), then available again. Only `nfs` and `hostPath` support it.

blocks.text: Manual reclaim of a Retained volume: delete the PV (the storage asset remains), clean up the data, then delete the asset or create a new PV for it.

items: Dynamically provisioned PVs **inherit** their StorageClass's reclaim policy, which defaults to **Delete**.
For Recycle, the docs recommend **dynamic provisioning** instead.

blocks.text: A unit's spec sheet lists its size (`capacity.storage`, the only resource you can set), its open modes, its reclaim policy and its catalog label (`storageClassName`). A labelled unit only rents to requests asking for that label; an unlabelled one only to requests asking for none. `volumeMode: Block` hands over a raw device instead of a folder. The unit's status board shows Available, Bound, Released or Failed.

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: <pv-name>
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: <size>
  volumeMode: Filesystem      # or Block
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: <class>
  mountOptions: [<option>]
  nfs:
    path: <export-path>
    server: <server>

items: `capacity.storage` is currently the **only** resource you can set or request.
`volumeMode`: `Filesystem` (the default) mounts a directory; `Block` gives the Pod a **raw block device**, used via `volumeDevices`/`devicePath` instead of a mount path.
`storageClassName`: a PV with a class only binds to PVCs requesting that class; a PV with no class only binds to PVCs requesting no class.
`mountOptions` aren't validated; a bad option makes the mount fail. `nodeAffinity` is required for `local` volumes.

rows: Claim deleted; resource not yet reclaimed

sections.heading: Writing a claim and using it

blocks.text: A rental request names a size, open modes and a catalog label, and the bay simply cites the request by name (`claimName`). Add a `selector` to narrow which units qualify, though then the catalog can't build one on demand. `volumeName` reserves a specific unit; if someone else has it, you wait. `storageClassName: ""` means "unlabelled units only", while leaving it unset lets the default catalog apply.

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: <pvc-name>
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  volumeMode: Filesystem
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: <size>
  storageClassName: <class>
---
# in the Pod spec
volumes:
- name: <volume-name>
  persistentVolumeClaim:
    claimName: <pvc-name>

items: `selector` (`matchLabels` / `matchExpressions`) narrows which PVs can bind. A PVC with a non-empty selector **can't** be dynamically provisioned.
`volumeName` pre-binds the claim to a specific PV. If that PV is bound to another PVC, the claim stays **pending**.
`storageClassName: ""` means "PVs with no class". Leaving the field **unset** lets the default StorageClass apply.
For Filesystem volumes the request is the outer size, so usable space can be slightly smaller.

sections.heading: Walkthrough: hostPath PV to Pod
sections.sourceTitle: Configure a Pod to Use a PersistentVolume for Storage

blocks.text: Walk through it on a one-ship port. The admin builds a 10Gi unit labelled `manual`; it shows Available. You file a 3Gi request with the same label, and the unit flips to Bound, your request now holding the full 10Gi. A bay mounts the request, never naming the unit. To tidy up, remove the bay, then the request, then the unit.
The official tutorial (single-node cluster) shows the full static flow. hostPath PVs are for development and testing only.

kubectl apply -f https://k8s.io/examples/pods/storage/pv-volume.yaml   # 10Gi, RWO, class manual
kubectl get pv task-pv-volume       # STATUS Available
kubectl apply -f https://k8s.io/examples/pods/storage/pv-claim.yaml    # requests 3Gi, class manual
kubectl get pv task-pv-volume       # STATUS Bound, CLAIM default/task-pv-claim
kubectl get pvc task-pv-claim       # CAPACITY 10Gi
kubectl apply -f https://k8s.io/examples/pods/storage/pv-pod.yaml

items: The claim asked for 3Gi but shows **10Gi**: it bound to the whole PV.
Matching used the same `storageClassName` (`manual`) plus size and access mode.
The Pod names only the **claim**, never the PV.
Clean up in order: `kubectl delete pod <pod>`, then `kubectl delete pvc <pvc>`, then `kubectl delete pv <pv>`.

blocks.text: Verify binding with `kubectl get pv <pv>` and `kubectl get pvc <pvc>`: the PV goes from `Available` to `Bound` and its CLAIM column shows `<namespace>/<pvc>`. The claim only binds to a PV with the same `storageClassName` that satisfies its size and access mode.

flashcards.front: PV vs PVC in one line each?
flashcards.back: PV: a piece of cluster storage (cluster resource, like a node). PVC: a user's request for storage (like a Pod consuming resources).

flashcards.front: What does a claim with `storageClassName: ""` do?
flashcards.back: Requests a PV with no class, so it opts out of dynamic provisioning.

flashcards.front: What happens to a PVC when no PV matches?
flashcards.back: It stays unbound indefinitely and binds once a matching PV appears.
RWO: read-write by a single node (several Pods on that node OK). RWOP: read-write by a single Pod cluster-wide; CSI only.

flashcards.front: CLI abbreviations of the four access modes?
flashcards.back: RWO = ReadWriteOnce, ROX = ReadOnlyMany, RWX = ReadWriteMany, RWOP = ReadWriteOncePod.

flashcards.front: Retain: what state is the PV in after its PVC is deleted?
flashcards.back: Released. Data stays and the PV can't be claimed again until an admin reclaims it.

flashcards.front: Which reclaim policy is deprecated, and which volume types still support it?
Default reclaim policy of a dynamically provisioned PV?
flashcards.back: Whatever its StorageClass sets; a StorageClass defaults to Delete.
Filesystem (default); Block exposes a raw block device.

flashcards.front: Which finalizer shows a PVC is protected from deletion while in use?
Can a Pod use a PVC from another namespace?
flashcards.back: No. Claims must be in the same namespace as the Pod.

flashcards.front: Tutorial: a 3Gi PVC binds to a 10Gi PV. What capacity does the PVC show?
flashcards.back: 10Gi — the claim gets the whole PV (at least what it asked for).

questions.stem: Which statement about PVs and PVCs is correct?

options.text: A PV is a cluster resource; a PVC is a namespaced request for storage
options.explanation: PVs are like nodes, PVCs like Pods consuming resources.

options.text: A PVC is created by the admin; a PV is created by the user
options.explanation: It's typically the other way round (or the PV is dynamically provisioned).

options.text: A PV is deleted automatically when its Pod is deleted
options.explanation: A PV's lifecycle is independent of any Pod.

options.text: A Pod references a PV directly by name in its volumes
options.explanation: Pods reference the claim (`claimName`), not the PV.

questions.stem: A PVC requests 100Gi, but the cluster only has 50Gi PVs and no dynamic provisioning. What happens?

options.text: The PVC stays unbound until a matching PV (100Gi or more) is added
options.explanation: Claims remain unbound indefinitely until a match exists.
Binding is one-to-one.

options.text: It binds to a 50Gi PV and grows it
options.explanation: A claim always gets at least what it asked for.

options.text: The PVC is rejected by the API server
options.explanation: It's created and stays Pending.

questions.stem: Which access modes allow read-write from more than one Pod? Select 2.

options.explanation: Read-write by many nodes.

options.text: ReadWriteOnce, when the Pods are on the same node
options.explanation: RWO is per node, so several Pods on that node can use it.
Only a single Pod in the whole cluster.
Many nodes, but read-only.

questions.stem: You must guarantee only one Pod in the whole cluster can write to a CSI-backed PVC. Which access mode?

options.explanation: RWOP restricts the volume to a single Pod; CSI only.
RWO restricts to a single node, not a single Pod.
Read-only.
Allows many nodes.

questions.stem: True or false: A PV created as ReadOnlyMany is guaranteed to be read-only once mounted.

options.explanation: Access modes are for matching; apart from RWOP they don't enforce write protection after mounting.
Correct — the docs say ROX gives no such guarantee.

questions.stem: A PV with `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain` has its PVC deleted. What is its state?

options.text: Released; the data remains and an admin must reclaim it manually
options.explanation: Retain keeps the PV and the data.

options.text: Available, ready for the next claim
options.explanation: The previous claimant's data is still there, so it isn't reusable yet.

options.text: Deleted together with the backing storage
options.explanation: That's the Delete policy.
Failed means automatic reclamation failed.

questions.stem: What is the default reclaim policy of a PV that was dynamically provisioned from a StorageClass that doesn't set reclaimPolicy?

options.explanation: Dynamically provisioned PVs inherit the class's policy, which defaults to Delete.
Only if the class sets it.
Recycle is deprecated and not a default.
There is a default.

questions.stem: Which statements about the Recycle reclaim policy are true? Select 2.

options.text: It is deprecated in favour of dynamic provisioning
options.explanation: Stated in the warning.

options.text: Only nfs and hostPath volume types support it
options.explanation: Stated for current Kubernetes.

options.text: It deletes the backing storage asset
options.explanation: That's Delete; Recycle scrubs files and reuses the volume.
The default is Delete.

questions.stem: Which PV phase means the claim was deleted but the storage hasn't been reclaimed yet?

options.explanation: Exactly that definition.
Free and not yet bound.
Still bound to a claim.
Automatic reclamation failed.

questions.stem: A PVC sets `selector.matchLabels` and names a StorageClass with a working provisioner, but no existing PV matches. What happens?

options.text: It stays unbound: a PVC with a non-empty selector can't be dynamically provisioned
options.explanation: The docs note this limitation.

options.text: A new PV is provisioned with those labels
options.explanation: Selectors block dynamic provisioning.

options.text: The selector is ignored and a PV is provisioned
options.explanation: It isn't ignored.

options.text: It binds to any PV in the class
options.explanation: Selector and class requirements are ANDed.

questions.stem: You delete a PVC that a running Pod still uses. What do you see?

options.text: The PVC shows Terminating with the kubernetes.io/pvc-protection finalizer until no Pod uses it
options.explanation: Storage Object in Use Protection postpones removal.

options.text: The PVC is removed and the Pod crashes
options.explanation: Removal is postponed to avoid data loss.

options.text: The deletion is rejected with an error
options.explanation: It's accepted but postponed.
The PV stays bound while the PVC exists.

questions.stem: True or false: A Pod can mount a PVC that lives in a different namespace if it gives the full name.

options.explanation: Claims must be in the same namespace as the Pod.
Correct.

questions.stem: A PV uses `volumeMode: Block`. How does a container access it?

options.explanation: Raw block devices use a device path, not a mount path.
That's for Filesystem mode.
Mount options tune how the volume is mounted; they don't expose a raw device.

options.text: It can't be used by Pods
options.explanation: Block mode is for applications that handle raw devices.

questions.stem: In the official tutorial, which field makes the PVC `task-pv-claim` bind to `task-pv-volume`?

options.text: Both use `storageClassName: manual`, and the size and access mode fit
options.explanation: The control plane looks for a PV with the same StorageClass that satisfies the claim.
It requests 3Gi; a bigger PV still satisfies it.
The Pod names only the claim.

options.text: A selector on the PVC matches the PV's `type: local` label
options.explanation: The tutorial's PVC has no selector; the label is just metadata here.
